article.title: Regression to the Mean: Why Extreme Customers Often Look More Normal Next Time
article.why: Practical analytical English with higher-difficulty emphasis.

paragraphs.en:
Regression to the mean is easy to confuse with a real improvement or deterioration. The problem appears when people are selected because their first measurement was unusually high or unusually low. Extreme observations often contain both a persistent component and temporary noise. When the temporary component does not repeat, the next measurement naturally moves closer to the average.

Consider a retailer that identifies the top 1 percent of customers by annual spending and gives them a special program. The following year, their average spending falls. It is tempting to conclude that the program failed or that loyalty weakened. Yet some customers entered the top 1 percent because of one-time events: a large appliance purchase, a family celebration, moving expenses, or simply random timing. Even without any intervention, many of them would have spent less the next year. The reverse can happen with extremely low-spending customers. Some will improve simply because the temporary problems that pushed them down disappear.

This is why before-and-after comparisons are risky when the sample is chosen using an extreme baseline. The expected counterfactual is not necessarily ‘the same extreme value again.’ A stronger design uses a comparable control group selected under the same rule. If both treatment and control groups regress toward the mean, the difference between them is more informative about the intervention. Repeated historical measurements also help. A customer who has ranked in the top decile for four consecutive years is more likely to have persistently high value than someone who appeared there once.

Regression to the mean also affects schools, hospitals, sports teams, investment funds, and operational quality metrics. Poor performers may look better after being singled out, while outstanding performers may look worse. This does not mean interventions never work. It means analysts must separate natural statistical reversion from causal impact.

A careful report might say, ‘Spending among last year’s top 1 percent declined this year, but part of the decline is expected from regression to the mean; treatment impact should be estimated relative to a matched or randomized comparison group.’ That wording preserves the observation without claiming a mechanism that the data cannot establish. The issue becomes even more important when organizations repeatedly target extremes. Suppose a quality team investigates the worst ten stores every month. Because some stores were unusually bad due to temporary staffing shortages, weather, or random variation, several will improve next month even if management changes nothing. If the team credits every improvement to its intervention, it will overestimate its effectiveness. Likewise, if a company rewards the highest-performing salespeople and their results fall afterward, the decline does not necessarily prove that the reward reduced motivation.

One practical safeguard is to examine the relationship between baseline extremeness and subsequent change before evaluating the intervention. If more extreme observations tend to show larger reversals even in untreated historical data, that pattern is evidence that regression to the mean is present. Analysts can also use multiple baseline periods, shrink noisy individual estimates toward a group average, or model persistent and temporary components separately. These methods reduce the chance of treating a one-period spike as a stable characteristic.

Communication matters because regression to the mean is often counterintuitive. Stakeholders may see a dramatic before-and-after chart and assume that the event in the middle caused the change. The analyst should explain that selection itself creates an expectation of movement. The more extreme the selection rule, and the noisier the measurement, the stronger that tendency can be. A useful question is: ‘What would we expect these units to look like next period if we did absolutely nothing?’ Without that benchmark, improvement among the worst performers and deterioration among the best performers can both be misread.
paragraphs.zh:
【重點翻譯】均值回歸最容易在「先挑極端值，再看前後變化」時被誤認成施策效果。極高消費者之所以進入 top 1%，一部分可能是穩定的高價值，一部分可能只是一次性大額購買、特殊事件或隨機波動。這些暫時因素下一期不一定重現，因此即使完全不做 intervention，平均值也常會往整體平均靠近。反過來，極低表現者也可能自然改善。

所以，若先挑出 worst stores、top customers 或最高績效者，再看到下一期回落或改善，不能直接把變化歸因於中間的措施。較好的方法是使用同樣篩選規則下的 control group、觀察多期歷史表現，或用 shrinkage 把噪音較大的極端估計拉回群體平均。真正應問的是：如果什麼都不做，這些極端個體下一期原本就會變成什麼樣？
paragraphs.ja:
【重点訳】平均への回帰は、「極端な値で対象を選び、その後の変化を見る」ときに施策効果と混同されやすい。top 1%の顧客には、恒常的に高価値な人だけでなく、一時的な大型購入や偶然で極端値になった人も含まれる。一時要因が繰り返されなければ、何もしなくても次期の平均は全体平均へ近づきやすい。

そのためworst storeやtop customerを選んだ後の改善・悪化を、直ちにinterventionの効果と解釈してはいけない。同じ選定条件のcontrol group、複数期間の履歴、shrinkageなどを使い、「何もしなかった場合にも起こる変化」と比較する必要がある。

vocabulary.usage: The central statistical mechanism in the article.
Describes unusually high or low observations.
Contrasts stable signal with temporary noise.
Describes nonpersistent causes of extreme values.
Refers to what would happen without intervention.
Provides a comparison for natural reversion.
Reduces overreaction to noisy extreme estimates.
The action whose causal effect must be separated from reversion.

business.term: Ask what would happen if we did nothing.
business.explanation: 先建立不介入時的合理基準。

business.term: Do not credit natural reversion to the intervention.
business.explanation: 不要把自然回歸錯算成施策效果。

sources: Background: regression to the mean, randomized comparison, repeated measures, and shrinkage estimation.
